Pollution fears after 350 drones fall into river in Melbourne lightshow fail
item.description:
Score 34 | Comments 14 (thread link) | @gsatic
July 19, 2023 | https://www.theage.com.au/national/victoria/extremely-concerning-yarra-battery-pollution-fears-after-drone-show-fail-20230716-p5dol8.html | archive.org

Yarra battery pollution fears after 350 drones fall into river in lightshow fail

We’re sorry, this feature is currently unavailable. We’re working to restore it. Please try again later.

Skip to sections navigationSkip to contentSkip to footer

A lightshow that ended when up to 350 drones ditched into Melbourne’s Yarra River has sparked concerns about how environmental risks were managed as efforts got underway to retrieve hundreds of lithium batteries from the water on the weekend.

Divers started searching Victoria Harbour in Docklands for the drones on Sunday morning after a lightshow at the Matildas’ warm-up clash with France at Marvel Stadium on Friday went haywire.

Videos posted to social media appear to show most of the 500 drones, operated by the Australian Traffic Network, entering auto-land mode and falling into the water. The company said there was no safety risk to the public.

But Charlotte Sterrett, who leads the Yarra Riverkeeper Association’s advocacy to protect the river’s health, said it was unacceptable that several hundred lithium batteries were polluting the river.

“Those batteries have metals such as cobalt, nickel and manganese, which are toxic and can contaminate water supplies and ecosystems,” she said. “There’s going to be immediate impacts on the ecosystem and all the animals and plants that live there, so it’s extremely concerning.”

Sterrett said it was vital that all drones were recovered and that similar shows did not take place over water until there was an assurance the same thing would not happen again.

“I do wonder what the risk management plan was. This shouldn’t have happened in the first place and we need to learn from that,” she said.

Australian Traffic Network’s Victorian CEO, Vic Lorusso, said the company lost around 350 of its drones and was still investigating what went wrong. The drones did the correct thing by entering auto-land and hitting the water when they encountered the glitch and there was never any safety risk to the public, he said.

“We’ve got five professional divers and our main focus is to retrieve as many drones as we can; we’re hopeful we can retrieve most of them,” Lorusso said. “It’s the only glitch we’ve seen in 18 months running the business ... so we’re trying to get to the bottom of it quickly.”

Fifty drones were also lost in the Swan River in Perth during a light show in November.

Greg Tyrrell, executive director of the Australian Association for Uncrewed Systems, a drone industry group, said it was highly unusual for so many drones to fall out of the sky during a lightshow performance and may have been the result of electromagnetic interference in the built-up Docklands district.

Loading

Tyrell said safety had been well managed by operating over water and having an exclusion zone in place, but the malfunction highlighted environmental and reputation issues the industry needed to address.

“You probably need to guarantee you have some way to recover the drones. Some systems float, for example — that’s one thing that probably needs to be looked at,” Tyrell said.

Robert Sutton, from Sydney-based drone consulting business Mirragin, said there were varying standards of drone systems and operators in Australia and tighter regulation would help ensure similar scenarios did not occur in the future.

Loading

“We are going to see incidents like this and they are a message we can’t ignore. We need to identify what went wrong and we need additional measures to address those kinds of things,” Sutton said.

A Civil Aviation Safety Authority spokesperson said the safety regulator had approved Friday night’s lightshow and was aware of how it turned out. “We are talking to the operator to understand what happened,” he said.

An Environment Protection Authority Victoria spokesperson said the agency was monitoring the situation.
